zh.question: 长得很像的两种细菌，一定做同样的事情吗？
zh.observe: 选择细胞壁、细胞膜、拟核与DNA、核糖体，对照整体标记和局部放大；在膜图追踪一次物质进出，再拖动生长与分裂进度，看看 DNA 复制发生在两个细胞分开之前。比较酸奶、土壤与肠道的不同作用。

academic.title: 细菌有自己的细胞组织
academic.body: 细菌是原核细胞，具有膜、细胞质、DNA与核糖体，拟核周围没有核膜。图中的肽聚糖细胞壁是支撑网，膜是选择性边界，两者不同；另一些细菌有外膜，少数缺少细胞壁。膜蛋白可帮助特定物质运输，但不同路线的能量和浓度条件不同。核糖体读取信使RNA来合成蛋白质。许多细菌通过二分裂增加数量：复制DNA、分配遗传信息并形成分隔，而不是像病毒那样在宿主内组装子代。

academic.title: 代谢把物质变化连接到生态作用
academic.body: 特定乳酸菌发酵乳中的糖产生乳酸，酸度变化帮助乳蛋白形成酸奶凝胶；某些土壤细菌参与分解和氮循环；肠道中的不同细菌利用不同底物。这些作用依赖酶与代谢途径，而不是“细菌”这个名字自动赋予的能力。同一环境的群落还与其他微生物交换物质，因此一个场景往往是多种生物共同活动的结果。

academic.title: 生长与影响都依赖具体条件
academic.body: 营养、可用水、温度、酸碱度和氧条件限制细菌生长，不同种类对氧的需求甚至相反。数量增长只在合适的一段条件内可能近似倍增，资源耗尽和代谢产物积累后会改变。对人的影响也与菌株、进入位置、数量和宿主状态有关，不能凭外形把它们永久分为好坏两类，更不能把认识有益菌理解为随意培养或食用未知菌。

zh.misconception: 细菌不是病毒，也不全是病菌；外形相似不保证能力或对人的影响相同。
zh.boundary: 主图只选较厚细胞壁的代表，颜色、数量和尺寸无测量含义。膜图只示意两条特定路线，分裂只演示一次，真实过程可重叠且速度不同；生活场景是不同群体，不能据此识别菌种或判断食品安全。

narration.label: 认识很小的细胞
narration.text: 说到细菌，你是不是先想到了生病？其实细菌有很多种，许多不会让人生病。看看这颗放大的细胞：外面的壁帮助撑住形状，里面的膜有选择地让一些物质进出。再往里，有保存信息的 DNA，也有制造蛋白质的小结构。点一下膜的按钮，停一停，追踪小小的营养物去了哪里。
narration.cue: 依次选择壁、膜、拟核与DNA、核糖体；回到膜，播放一次进出并在营养物越过膜后暂停。

narration.label: 酸奶里的变化
narration.text: 把场景切到酸奶。制作酸奶会用到挑选好的乳酸菌，它们利用奶里的糖，产生乳酸，帮助奶变得酸酸的、稠稠的。这里不是说随便找到一种细菌，都能做出好吃的酸奶。停一停，看看同一个细菌主题，已经和我们餐桌上的食物连起来了。

narration.label: 土里和身体里的邻居
narration.text: 再去土壤看看，一些细菌与真菌等伙伴一起，参与分解掉落的植物，让其中的物质重新流动。肠道里也有许多细菌，有些能处理我们不容易消化的食物成分。不同的细菌有不同本领，不是每一只都会做酸奶、分解落叶，又完成所有其他工作。
narration.cue: 依次显示土壤与肠道，突出不同作用。

narration.label: 从一颗到两颗
narration.text: 小细胞怎样变多呢？我们慢慢看一次。细胞长大，DNA 先复制出一份，两份信息分开，中间再形成分隔。现在有两个细胞了！它们还需要合适的水分、食物和环境，不能一直翻倍。认识这些小居民，也要记得：长得像，不代表本领一样，更不是让我们拿未知的东西来吃。
narration.cue: 播放一次生长与分裂；在 DNA 复制后暂停，再继续到两个子细胞，最后保持终态。

en.question: Must two bacteria with similar shapes do the same things?
en.observe: Select wall, membrane, nucleoid and DNA, and ribosomes. Compare the whole-cell marker with the enlarged detail. Follow one membrane exchange, then move the growth-and-division slider to see DNA copying before the two cells separate. Compare roles in yogurt, soil and the gut.

academic.title: Bacteria have cellular organisation
academic.body: Bacteria are prokaryotic cells with membranes, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes; the nucleoid has no nuclear membrane. The illustrated peptidoglycan wall provides supporting mesh, distinct from the selective membrane. Other bacteria have an outer membrane; a few lack a wall. Membrane proteins transport particular substances, with different energy and concentration requirements. Ribosomes read messenger RNA to make proteins. Many bacteria reproduce through binary fission, copying and partitioning DNA before separating, unlike viruses assembled within a host.

academic.title: Metabolism connects chemistry with ecological roles
academic.body: Selected lactic-acid bacteria ferment milk sugar and acidify it, helping proteins form yogurt gel. Other bacteria participate in decomposition, nitrogen transformations or gut metabolism. These abilities depend on particular pathways, not the label “bacterium”. Communities often exchange products with other microbes, so outcomes may arise from several organisms.

academic.title: Growth and effects depend on conditions
academic.body: Nutrients, available water, temperature, pH and oxygen limit growth, with differing oxygen requirements among bacteria. Approximate doubling does not continue indefinitely as resources and wastes change. Effects on a host depend on strain, location and circumstances rather than an organism’s drawn shape or a permanent good/bad label.

en.misconception: Bacteria are not viruses, and not all cause disease. Similar shapes do not guarantee similar abilities or effects.
en.boundary: The main cell represents one thick-walled type; colors, counts and dimensions are illustrative. Membrane exchange shows only two selected routes. Division runs once; real processes may overlap and have different timing. Habitats show different communities. These images cannot identify species or establish food safety.

narration.label: Meet a tiny cell
narration.text: Does the word bacteria make you think of illness? There are many kinds, and many do not make us ill. Look at this enlarged cell. Its outer wall helps hold its shape. Just inside, a membrane selectively lets some substances enter or leave. Further in are DNA that stores information and small structures that make proteins. Press the membrane button, pause, and follow where the tiny nutrient goes.
narration.cue: Select wall, membrane, nucleoid and DNA, and ribosomes. Return to the membrane, play one exchange and pause after the nutrient crosses it.

narration.label: A change in yogurt
narration.text: Switch to yogurt. Carefully selected lactic-acid bacteria use milk sugar and produce lactic acid, helping make yogurt tangy and thick. This does not mean any unknown bacterium can make suitable yogurt. Pause and notice how the tiny world connects with familiar food.
narration.cue: Pause at the yogurt scene for three seconds.

narration.label: Neighbours in soil and bodies
narration.text: Some soil bacteria work with fungi and others to break down plant remains and recycle materials. Many bacteria also live in the gut, including kinds that process food components we cannot easily digest. Different bacteria have different abilities; no single kind necessarily performs every job.

narration.label: From one cell to two
narration.text: How do little cells become more numerous? Let us watch once, slowly. The cell grows and makes a copy of its DNA. The two copies separate, and a partition forms between them. Now there are two cells! They still need suitable water, food and surroundings, so they cannot keep doubling forever. Remember, similar shapes do not mean the same abilities, and learning about these residents does not mean tasting unknown things.
narration.cue: Play one growth-and-division sequence. Pause after DNA copying, then continue until two daughter cells form and hold the final state.

references.title: OpenStax — Unique Characteristics of Prokaryotic Cells
